question_text: A 35-year-old soldier is rescued from a helicopter crash in the Arctic Circle and brought back to a treatment facility at a nearby military base. On arrival, the patient's wet clothes are removed. He appears pale and is not shivering. He is unresponsive to verbal and painful stimuli. His temperature is 27.4°C (81.3°F), pulse is 30/min and irregular, respirations are 7/min, and blood pressure is 83/52 mm Hg. Examination shows fixed, dilated pupils and diffuse rigidity. The fingers and toes are white in color and hard to the touch. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. In addition to emergent intubation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Question
                    A 35-year-old soldier is rescued from a helicopter crash in the Arctic Circle and brought back to a treatment facility at a nearby military base. On arrival, the patient's wet clothes are removed. He appears pale and is not shivering. He is unresponsive to verbal and painful stimuli. His temperature is 27.4°C (81.3°F), pulse is 30/min and irregular, respirations are 7/min, and blood pressure is 83/52 mm Hg. Examination shows fixed, dilated pupils and diffuse rigidity. The fingers and toes are white in color and hard to the touch. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation. In addition to emergent intubation, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Intravenous administration of tissue plasminogen activator
opb. Intravenous administration of diltiazem
opc. Application of heating pads to the extremities
opd. Intravenous administration of warmed normal saline
ope. Emergent electrical cardioversion

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient is experiencing severe hypothermia, indicated by a critically low body temperature of 27.4°C, unresponsiveness, bradycardia, and fixed, dilated pupils. Hypothermia can lead to cardiac arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation, as seen on the ECG. In this context, immediate management should focus on rewarming the patient and stabilizing hemodynamics. The administration of warmed normal saline is appropriate as it aids in rewarming and volume resuscitation, which can improve blood pressure and potentially stabilize the heart rhythm. Other options, such as tissue plasminogen activator or diltiazem, are not indicated in this scenario, and emergent electrical cardioversion is not the first step without addressing the underlying hypothermia. Therefore, the best next step in management is the intravenous administration of warmed normal saline.
